one_liner: SIMD C extension replacing CPython's json.dumps/loads; README claims 4-31x faster dumps and 2-8x faster loads.
what_it_does: A CPython extension module (C, plus C++ for the float formatter) exposing dumps (returns str), dumps_to_bytes (returns UTF-8 bytes) and loads (accepts str or bytes), with optional NumPy scalar/ndarray encoding after setup_numpy_types(np). It accepts json.dumps/json.loads keyword names so `import ssrjson as json` runs for code that only calls dumps/loads. Only indent (None, 2 or 4), object_hook and array_hook actually do anything; sort_keys, default, cls, separators, ensure_ascii, parse_float, parse_int and object_pairs_hook are accepted and ignored. Output is always compact with non-ASCII characters left unescaped, and there is no dump/load file API or JSONEncoder/JSONDecoder class.
how_it_is_fast: Strings are processed directly in CPython's internal PEP 393 layout (ASCII/UCS1/UCS2/UCS4) by hand-written SIMD kernels for escape scanning, copying and width conversion. On x86-64 it compiles three copies of the core (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512) and picks one at runtime; aarch64 uses NEON. dumps_to_bytes has its own SIMD UTF-8 encoder instead of CPython's cached PyUnicode_AsUTF8, and bytes input to loads is validated and transcoded with simdutf-style vector shapes plus Lemire's lookup4 UTF-8 validation, widening the output buffer in place. Floats are printed with xjb64/xjb32 shortest-round-trip formatting; integer printing, number parsing and the core parser come from yyjson; and object keys of 64 bytes or less are reused from a 512-slot xxHash64-indexed cache (orjson's short-key cache idea) to avoid allocating str objects.
when_to_use: CPython 3.10-3.14 services on x86-64-v2+ or aarch64 where json.dumps/json.loads of plain dict/list/str/int/float/bool/None data shows up in profiles, and the code calls them with default options.
Encode-heavy workloads producing str: the v0.0.17 charts show dumps-to-str 7.5x (twitter.json) to 23x (canada.json) faster than json, and 1.2-2.0x ahead of orjson on the same charts.

Emitting UTF-8 bytes of non-ASCII text such as CJK strings: dumps_to_bytes on simple_object_zh.json is charted at 6.55x json vs 1.46x for orjson when the str objects have no UTF-8 cache (a fast-path probe, not real-world data).

Float/number-heavy documents and NumPy arrays: canada.json loads is 7.75x json vs orjson 4.28x on the charts, and the README's NumPy microbenchmark shows ndarray dumps_to_bytes 1.4-10x faster than orjson.
Parsing JSON that is already a Python str: loads(str) skips UTF-8 transcoding (twitter.json 2.54x json vs orjson 1.80x).
when_not_to_use: Code that relies on json options: sort_keys, default=, cls, separators, ensure_ascii=True, parse_float/parse_int and object_pairs_hook are ignored, and indent accepts only 2 or 4. Output ordering and escaping will differ from json.

Data outside the JSON core types: dict keys that are not str raise JSONEncodeError (json turns int keys into strings); datetime, dataclass, UUID, Decimal and similar objects raise 'Unsupported type to encode' with no default hook; ints outside the int64/uint64 range fail in dumps and silently become float in loads.

32-bit targets, x86-64-v1 CPUs without SSE4.2, big-endian machines, PyPy or other non-CPython runtimes. musl Linux, glibc older than 2.34, Intel macOS and Python 3.15 get no wheel, so they must build from source with Clang and CMake 3.30+.

Risk-averse production: the project is beta (0.0.x, PyPI 'Development Status :: 4 - Beta'), has 39 stars, and 2026 releases fixed several memory-safety bugs (a NEON encoder heap overflow in 0.0.19 that 'all prior versions' should upgrade past, 1-byte heap overflows in 0.0.20/0.0.21, invalid reads in 0.0.23), although fuzzing and ASAN run in CI.

Free-threaded CPython with containers shared across threads: support is experimental. The encoder locks dicts/lists outer-to-inner and can deadlock against other lock orders, and the optional lock-free build crashes on concurrent mutation.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond CPython (NumPy optional, enabled explicitly via setup_numpy_types). Source build needs Clang (clang-cl on Windows), CMake >= 3.30 and C17/C++20; yyjson-derived code, xjb, xxHash and khash are vendored.
integration.min_toolchain: CPython 3.10+ (PyPI wheels for 3.10-3.14 and 3.14t; 3.15 is source-only). Source builds require Clang (minimum version not documented); GCC and plain MSVC are rejected by CMake.
integration.platforms: x86-64-v2+ (SSE4.2 minimum; runtime dispatch to SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512) and aarch64 (NEON), 64-bit little-endian only. Wheels: manylinux_2_34 x86-64/aarch64, macOS arm64, Windows amd64.
integration.thread_safety: GIL builds: safe to call from any thread; the global decode buffers and key cache rely on the GIL. Free-threaded 3.14t builds: experimental, with per-thread buffers and key cache and lock-based encoding (deadlock possible under conflicting lock orders); decoding is lock-free. Settings such as write_utf8_cache and strict_argparse are process-global.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — `import ssrjson as json` works for dumps/loads with default arguments, but output is compact and unescaped (like separators=(',',':'), ensure_ascii=False), most kwargs are ignored, non-str keys and ints wider than 64 bits are rejected or converted to float, and there is no dump/load, JSONEncoder or JSONDecoder.

gotchas: Unsupported kwargs are ignored, not rejected: dumps(obj, sort_keys=True) returns unsorted output and prints only a one-time stderr warning ('some options are not supported'). Call ssrjson.strict_argparse(True) to turn these into errors.

dumps_to_bytes writes CPython's per-str UTF-8 cache by default, so each non-ASCII str encoded keeps an extra UTF-8 copy alive until the str is freed. For one-shot encodes, disable it with ssrjson.write_utf8_cache(False) or is_write_cache=False. dumps_to_bytes also rejects lone surrogates (U+D800-DFFF), which dumps passes through.

loads turns out-of-range integers into float without an error, accepts NaN/Infinity in any letter case (but not 'inf'), and stops at 1024 levels of nesting (encode as well). object_hook/array_hook re-entrancy is capped at 32 nested decoder levels.

Memory footprint: each decoding context carries about 1 MB of scratch (two 512 KB string buffers), and the key cache holds references to up to 512 short key str objects between calls. Free-threaded builds allocate this per thread.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over orjson, the other catalogued stdlib-json replacement, when you want json-style call signatures and str output, encode a lot of non-ASCII text or numeric/NumPy data, or want control over the UTF-8 cache: the same first-party charts put it 1.2-2.0x ahead of orjson on dumps-to-str and 1.1-1.8x on loads. Stay with orjson if you need default=, OPT_SORT_KEYS/OPT_NON_STR_KEYS, native datetime/dataclass/UUID serialization, x86-64-v1/32-bit/musl wheels or a more mature project; simdjson and yyjson are C/C++ parsers rather than Python modules, and ssrJSON reuses yyjson's parser and number code.
verified_claims_summary: These are first-party ssrjson-benchmark charts for v0.0.17 on Python 3.14 and an unnamed x86-64 AVX2 CPU; the Clang version and build flags for the measured ssrJSON are not stated, and the harness pins one core and interleaves libraries against stdlib json with compact separators. They show dumps-to-str 4.9x (simple_object_zh) to 23.1x (canada) and loads(str) 2.5x (twitter) to 7.8x (canada) faster than json, which the README rounds to 4-31x and 2-8x, with orjson at 1.80x (twitter loads str) and 16.67x (canada dumps str) on the same charts.
status_note: Actively maintained: 0.0.23 was released to PyPI on 2026-09-17, the same day as the last commit, and CI runs fuzzing and ASAN. It is still a beta 0.0.x project (39 stars, mostly one author with 230 of 246 commits), MIT-licensed and easiest to consume as PyPI wheels, since vendoring or source builds require Clang.
